pr_body:
We introduced forking in AbstractSearchAsyncAction to prevent StackOverflow, which could happen when the method `performPhaseOnShard` was responded on the same thread and it executed the next shard requests recursively.

This commit removes that forking by never let the responding thread execute the next shard requests unless it is different than the calling thread, and let the caller executes all possible shard requests instead of a single request.

Closes #70792
pr_comment: /cc @jtibshirani as you are working on search resiliency.
@javanna @jimczi Sorry for the late response. I think it's ready again. Would you mind taking another look? Thank you!

I'm on the fence whether addressing #70792 in this way is making sense. As the search thread pool is used in various ways (shard-level search requests, as well as occasionally during coordination and reduce phases on the coordinating node), looking at the number of tasks queued up there might not necessarily be a reflection of actual "search" work load, but is just an odd way of limiting the number of outstanding tasks (where tasks that are completely different in nature are mixed, which is also confusing in the context of Adaptive Replica Selection). I would love to separate these usages of the thread pool more cleanly, perhaps having separate executors for lightweight coordination-level / can-match stuff vs actual shard-level search work or merge work.

I also find it odd that we can fail during the merge phase (see `QueryPhaseResultConsumer`) when enqueuing something on the search executor just because the node seems to be hit with a lot of search requests (i.e. we fail completing a search just because another search is coming in). If we fix that, there is yet another case where there can be more tasks enqueued on the search thread pool than configured.

On the indexing side, we encountered similar challenges and have stepped away from limiting indexing via the write queue size (where we also forced things onto the queue under certain circumstances), but instead built a separate mechanism (called indexing pressure) that does this memory-based and more accurately tracks the lifecycle of requests, separating coordination aspects more cleanly from internal shard-level tasks. If there's interest, we can explore a similar approach here.
Closing this as we will introduce a new thread pool for search coordination.

review_comment: It seems costly to have a loop that runs until a semaphore is acquired ? Won't that block the network thread when lots of shards are co-located on the same node and the max shard execution is low ?
